TUSTARI:91:4/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:91:4/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:91:4/r1.claim: Inwardly, night is sin and persistence in sin covering faith’s light so it does not shine in the heart or appear in a person’s qualities.

TUSTARI:91:4/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:91:4/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TUSTARI:91:4/r2.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying that appetite and desire overcome knowledge and reason.

TAB-FULL:v24p437#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p437#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p437#2/r1.claim: Night covers the sun until it sets and the horizons become dark; Qatadah gives the same gloss.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436/r2.speaker: يزيد بن ذي حمامة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436/r2.claim: Yazid ibn Dhi Hamama reports a saying that night veils people with God's great creation, but the Creator deserves still greater awe.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r13.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r13.speaker: يزيد بن ذي حمامة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r13.claim: Yazid ibn Dhi Hamama says that night inspires awe, but its Creator is more worthy of reverence.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r4.claim: Mujahid says the night covers the sun.

NAHHAS:v5p235/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p235/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p235/r4.claim: The pronoun refers to the sun.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p212#3/r7.claim: Night covers the sun until it sets and the horizons become dark.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r16.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r16.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r16.claim: Mujahid explains the night covering the sun as making it dark.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r17.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r17.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r17.claim: Mawardi also takes the night to conceal the sun and cites a verse by al-Khansa for this usage.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r4.claim: Night covers the sun when it sets and darkens the horizons.

KASHSHAF:91:4/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:4/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:4/r1.claim: The pronoun may refer to darkness, the world, or the earth, although earth was not previously mentioned; ordinary speech similarly omits understood referents such as morning or sky.

KASHSHAF:91:4/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:4/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:4/r2.claim: The night covers its referent until it disappears and the horizons grow dark.

KASHSHAF:91:4/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:4/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:4/r3.claim: The accusative of idhā is difficult: coordination seems to govern both accusative and genitive, while treating each wāw as oath conflicts with al-Khalil and Sibawayh's aversion.

KASHSHAF:91:4/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:4/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:4/r4.claim: The oath wāw suppresses the verb and itself stands in its place, unlike bāʾ, which replaces both verb and preposition; coordinated wāws can therefore govern both cases, as in a verb's coordination.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r4.claim: The night veils the sun, making the horizons dark; the implied object may be inferred just as ‘it became cold’ can imply morning and ‘it rained’ can imply the sky.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.claim: The repeated wāws can govern both accusative and genitive: the oath-wāw omits its verb altogether and substitutes for it, while coordinated wāws inherit that double function, resolving the apparent two-governor problem.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:91:1-15/r10.claim: Night covers the sun until it sets, darkening the horizons and clothing it in darkness.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#2/r1.claim: Night covers the sun when it sets, darkening the horizons.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.claim: The sura urges obedience and warns against disobedience; oaths by beneficial created things prompt reflection and gratitude because divine oaths weigh heavily on the heart.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r1.claim: Night covers the sun and removes its light; this strengthens the reading that daytime reveals the sun by contrast, and the nearby pronouns then consistently refer to the sun.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.claim: Al-Qaffal says all four oaths are really about the sun through its midday light, the moon's borrowing its light, its emergence in daytime and its concealment at night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r3.claim: Reflecting on the sun's finite size and composite parts reveals its createdness and leads the mind to the Creator's greatness.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:4/r1.speaker: مجاهد وغيره
QURTUBI-FULL:91:4/r1.claim: Night covers the sun and removes its light when it sets.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:4/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:91:4/r2.claim: Alternatively, night covers the world with darkness and darkens the horizons; the pronoun refers to an unstated object.

BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r4.claim: Night covers the sun and its light, the horizons, or earth; the successive conjunctions link the oath phrases to their preceding grammatical elements.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r1.claim: Night covers the sun and darkens the horizons.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r2.claim: The first wāw in this oath sequence is unanimously understood as an oath particle; some also take the second wāw as an oath.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r3.speaker: الخليل
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r3.claim: Al-Khalil takes the second wāw as coordination, since introducing an oath before the first oath is complete is impermissible; replacing it with fa or thumma would leave the sense unchanged.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r4.claim: Those who treat the second wāw as an oath argue that coordination would attach a genitive noun to a noun governed by the oath wāw and an accusative temporal clause to one governed by the implicit verb 'I swear.'

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#7/r5.claim: The response is that the oath wāw functions like bāʾ plus its verb, as one governor with two cases, so one conjunction may coordinate both objects, as in the cited example.

QASHANI:91:1-3/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:91:1-3/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:91:1-3/r4.claim: The ego’s darkness covers spirit; the heart arises through their mixture, since darkness lets it discern meanings that pure spirit-light cannot retain, though all three are one reality named by rank.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.claim: The Meccan surah swears by parts of the upper and lower worlds and by the soul as an instrument of reflection; it moves from disbelievers' afterlife to their worldly destruction and eventual Fire.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r1.claim: Night veils the sun, making it disappear and darkening the horizons; attributing this to night is figurative.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r2.claim: One alternative makes the pronoun refer to the earth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.claim: For eloquence, all the pronouns through يغشاها should refer to the sun; this matches the preceding description of day revealing it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r4.claim: The imperfect يغشاها preserves the feminine-hā rhyme; the past would end غشيها and break the intended cadence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.speaker: القفال
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.claim: Al-Qaffāl summarizes the oaths as four solar aspects: daytime brightness and activity, the moon taking its light, full appearance, and disappearance at night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.speaker: أصحابنا
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.claim: The author's colleagues interpret سبحان من سخركن as a proper name, with mā infinitival and temporal.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.claim: The Shaykh invokes the Sibawayh poem as a case of coordinating a genitive plus nominative pair with another pair; the author says this concedes the disputed coordination, though the poem has an additional complication.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.claim: Al-Khalil says the last two wāws in the oath sequence coordinate nouns, while the first is like the prepositional wāw and the tā’ of swearing.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.speaker: ابن كيسان
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kaysan permits an explicit oath verb with the wāw, as in ‘I swear by God that Zayd is standing’; the author says this objection does not bind al-Zamakhshari’s position.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.claim: The Shaykh identifies the deeper puzzle as finding a governor for a future ‘idha’ after an oath: the present oath verb, an implied event, the oath object itself, and an implied circumstantial all face objections.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.claim: The Shaykh’s preference that conjunction does not itself govern does not compel al-Zamakhshari, who chooses the alternative grammatical doctrine.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.claim: The author insists that the construction does involve two governors: oath wāw governs the genitive and the oath verb governs the time adverb, with both sets of complements coordinated.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.claim: The Sibawayh poem cited by the Shaykh acknowledges coordination across the two governors, even though the Shaykh relies on Sibawayh’s authority.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.claim: Mentioning Ibn Kaysan’s permission to state an oath verb does not refute al-Zamakhshari, because the latter need not share Ibn Kaysan’s view.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.claim: The Shaykh’s example with a second time phrase preceding the coordinated noun does parallel the verse’s governors, though it raises a separate issue of repeating the construction.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.claim: Al-Khalil’s description as ‘disfavored’ supports prohibition rather than rebutting al-Zamakhshari; the Shaykh has either softened the term or misunderstood it.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.claim: An omitted construct such as ‘rising of the star’ can be the governor; the author says an oath now may refer to an object that will exist later, so the tense mismatch is no objection.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.claim: A deleted governor before ‘idha’ is possible as a prospective circumstantial; the oath verb still governs it, and the circumstantial may be understood prospectively.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.claim: If the sworn object is a physical entity, one can supply an event, making the temporal phrase a circumstantial attached to that event; Ibn al-Hajib addressed the question and the author notes extended debate.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.claim: The ‘idha’ clauses raise a syntactic problem: a conditional needs an answer, while a purely temporal phrase needs a governor; the oath verb is present-time and cannot straightforwardly govern a future time phrase.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that an oath wāw suppresses its verb and stands for both the verb and preposition; following coordinating wāws can therefore govern the same accusative and genitive pattern.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.claim: The Shaykh rejects the claim that a conjunction governs by standing in for a governor; he says the governor of the coordinated element is the same as for its antecedent, though he does not insist on that point against al-Zamakhshari.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.claim: The Shaykh says the verse coordinates two nouns with matching case roles, rather than coordinating across two governors, and offers ‘passing by Zayd standing and ‘Amr sitting’ as the pattern.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.claim: The Shaykh cites a line in Sibawayh that coordinates a genitive and a nominative with another genitive and nominative as a parallel construction.

SAMIN-DURR:91:4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:4/r1.claim: In ‘yaghshaha’, the object pronoun may refer to the sun or the earth.

SAMIN-DURR:91:4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:4/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:4/r2.claim: The present ‘yaghshaha’ replaces the past form used around it to maintain the verse endings; ‘idha ghashiyaha’ would break the sound pattern.

IBNKATHIR:91:4/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:4/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:91:4/r1.claim: Night covers the sun at its setting and darkens the horizons.

IBNKATHIR:91:4/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:4/r2.speaker: يزيد بن ذي حمامة
IBNKATHIR:91:4/r2.claim: When night comes, God says that night has covered His servants with His great creation; night fears it, though its Creator deserves even greater fear. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits the report.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r1.claim: Night is the day’s opposite: a realm of stillness, contraction, concealment, and latent things.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r2.claim: Night progressively covers the sun at sunset, extending the earth’s shadows and darkening the eastern horizon for longer or shorter periods.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r3.claim: Night’s fading light figures bodily nature veiling intellect through its corrupt temperament and poor constitution.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r4.claim: Night’s gradual covering contrasts with day, which reveals the sun at once when clouds and haze are absent.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r9.claim: The outward cosmos has an inward human counterpart, so celestial and terrestrial features can be read as faculties and bodily processes.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r11.speaker: يزيد بن ذي حمامة
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r11.claim: He reports God's address that night veils His creatures in His vast creation and inspires awe, while the Creator of night deserves greater awe.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.claim: He glossed the sun as its light, the moon as following it, daylight as illuminating it, God as builder of heaven, the earth as spread out, inspiration as showing good and evil, and corruption as leading astray.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.claim: Although the conditional sense of idha seems to require an answer and an operator, the author reads it causally in these oaths: swear because the moon follows, the day reveals, and the night covers; al-Qamus also allows a present-time meaning, “when.”

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r5.claim: Night is the earth's shadow between sun and observer; it figuratively covers the sun by hiding its light, or covers the horizons and earth.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r6.claim: The present verb indicates that God is not subject to time, so future is like past; it also suits the verse endings, and yaghsha is used because taghashiya takes two objects.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.claim: The oath wa's are conjunctive and share the implied verb, avoiding the problem of coordinating words governed by different agents or multiplying oaths with one answer.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r8.claim: In the inward reading, night is the ego's darkness covering the spirit's day; night manifests the name al-Mudill, just as day manifests the name al-Hadi.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r1.claim: The night covers the sun and hides its light; other views take the pronoun to mean Earth or the world.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r2.claim: Abu Hayyan says the present tense maintains the verse-ending rhyme; using ghāshāh would require omitting one of the verb's two objects.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r3.speaker: بعض الأجلة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r3.claim: Some scholars say the present tense indicates that all times are alike to God.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r4.speaker: الخفاجي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r4.claim: Al-Khafaji says night here is the darkness that arises after light, rather than original nonbeing; this more clearly manifests power and calls for the changed tense.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari sees a problem in governing each idha: coordination seems to join constituents governed by different operators, while treating each as an oath risks several oaths sharing one answer, which al-Khalil and Sibawayh disliked.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that the oath wāw stands for the oath verb and the later coordinating wāws inherit its genitive and accusative work, as in his example of striking several objects.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r7.claim: Alusi objects that the first conjunction has no accusative object and that conjunctions are not generally grammatical operators; other analyses also remove the difficulty by allowing coordination across operators or separate oath answers.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141#2/r8.claim: The objection also assumes idha must be temporal; it may instead be a substitute for its following noun, or be attached to omitted nouns such as the moon's following, the day's display, and night's covering.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r1.claim: The line about companions departing uses idha as a substitute for “tomorrow”; if idha remains temporal, omitted nouns for the moon's following, the day's display, and the night's covering can govern it.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r2.claim: The deeper analysis is that idha attaches to an omitted noun such as “greatness,” since oaths honor their objects and are not temporally restricted; objections to this analysis are answered by the figurative force of the oath.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p142/r3.claim: Alusi rejects the claim that this omitted-noun analysis is redundant even if the oath itself is figurative, because there would otherwise be no syntactic element to which the intended emphasis attaches.

ELMALILI:91:4/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:4/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:4/r1.claim: The oath concerns night as it covers the sun and horizons, obscuring light in the onset or continuation of dense darkness.

ELMALILI:91:4/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:4/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:4/r2.claim: The contrast with daylight reveals the importance of light and the value of inner awareness that feels its absence when outward light is gone.

ELMALILI:91:4/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:4/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:4/r3.claim: The darkness alludes to the moon's obscuration and to the soul veiled from divine guidance by ignorance, disbelief, grief, heedlessness, inertia, or desire, as well as to death's moment.

ELMALILI:91:4/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:4/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:4/r4.claim: The earlier oaths carry glad tidings, whereas this oath about darkness has a warning character.

ELMALILI:91:4/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:4/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:4/r5.claim: The shift from past forms for the preceding oaths to a present-future form here emphasizes darkness at its initial attack and while it persists.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:4/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:4/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:4/r1.claim: Night’s covering is the opposite of daylight’s disclosure: it envelops and hides everything, affecting both the human psyche and human life.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.claim: The oath confirms the threat of destruction implicitly conveyed by the news; each waw following a pause is an oath particle, and the sun, moon, sky, earth, and human soul display God's wise and powerful creation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.claim: The dawn brightness, moon following the sun, daylight, and night are all examples of the fine order God established.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r1.claim: Night does not literally cover the sun; it results from half the Earth covering the sun's disk after sunset. Attributing the action to night is a rational metaphor by time or cause; Earth's rotation is the real covering, though the feminine pronoun may instead refer to Earth as with the daylight clause.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.claim: إذا is a circumstantial time adverb attached to the state of each moon, day, and night; each is sworn by in the condition that best displays God's artistry.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r4.claim: Tying the night oath to its covering moment recalls the lesson of darkness arising after light.

TABATABAI:91:1-8/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r6.claim: The night covers earth, as in the preceding verse; taking the object as the sun is implausible because night covers earth and what is upon it.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qur'anic oaths probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though the connection remains insufficiently researched.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.claim: The structure and function of cumulative oath series are discussed at 93:1–2, with many parallels.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.claim: An eight-verse oath series leads into the antithetical statement in verses 9–10; the pre-Islamic genre is repurposed in verses 5–7 to express biblical creation ideas.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.claim: The series moves through three complementary or contrasting pairs—sun/moon, night/day, heaven/earth—then the soul, whose opposed moral capacities are specified in verse 8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.claim: The oath series narrows from cosmic creation, traced vertically from celestial bodies to earth, to the human moral subject.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.claim: Its shift from creation to humanity resembles the 81:1–14 sequence, which evokes the world's eschatological dissolution rather than cyclical operation.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.claim: A caesura after verse 4 divides effects and activities of the oath's objects in verses 1–4 from references to God's creating activity in verses 5–8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.claim: The translation signals paired oaths by beginning verses 2, 4, and 6 with and, following Neuwirth.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.claim: One might translate talā as the moon falling behind the sun, but the parallel between verses 1–3 and 2–4 favors the moon's following the day into night.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r1.claim: The wording is closely related to 92:1–2, pairing night with yaġšā and day with tajallā or jallā.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.claim: The world appears to contain opposing forces, yet God keeps them within limits and in harmony; their accord preserves the universe.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night are complementary phenomena; their apparent oppositions in appearance, temperament, and effects serve in harmony.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.claim: Earlier sūrahs used this complementarity for arguments about monotheism and the Day of Judgement; here the focus is how the apparent opposites work together.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.claim: The cosmic order prevents the sun or moon from intruding on the other’s appointed time and keeps day and night within their roles, as 36:40 says.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.claim: Harmony among opposites sustains the universe; their obedience to limits teaches people to stay within God’s bounds, since exceeding them creates disorder God will not tolerate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.claim: Some take 91:9–10 as the oath’s complement; Islahi gives weight to al-Zamakhsharī’s rejection of that view.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night show that a powerful, self-sustaining God keeps the world’s elements on their appointed paths, preventing their collision from destroying it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.claim: Suppressing the complement lets everything evident from the oaths count as its content; one prominent implication is that God destroys rebellious nations.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.claim: Oaths by natural phenomena highlight cosmic order and its benefits, the Creator's power, and the importance of what follows.

STUDYQURAN:91:4/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:4/r1.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:91:4/r1.claim: The night may be understood as enshrouding the sun.

STUDYQURAN:91:4/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:4/r2.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:91:4/r2.claim: The night may instead be understood as enshrouding the world.

STUDYQURAN:91:4/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:4/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:91:4/r3.claim: Spiritually, sins that persist cover the light of faith.
